text.p: The European Commission counter- attacked on Tuesday against German allegations that it had mishandled the mad cow crisis and that EU veterinary experts did not listen to scientific evidence.

Last week a German animal feed expert, Oscar Riedinger, criticised the Commission for failing to insist on higher standards for processing meat and bone meal, which is held responsible for spreading mad cow disease.

Riedinger told the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into the disease, known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), that EU experts should have advised that the meat and bone meal be treated at a higher temperature.
"The accusation is untrue, is false and the whole attack is somewhat misguided," Lars Hoelgaard, head of the Commission's animal health directorate, told a news conference.
The crisis broke in March after the British government admitted that the fatal cattle brain disease could be passed to people who ate infected beef.
Scared shoppers shunned beef and switched to white meat, such as pork and poultry, sending beef prices plunging and ruining livestock farmers across the continent.
Hoelgaard, the Commission's link with the parliament committee, said only high risk cattle parts, such as brain and spinal cord, were subjected to high pressure heat and chemical processing.
Low risk cattle or sheep tissue, whether in Britain or in other EU member states, including Germany, was not subject to such stringent processing standards, he added.
"Therefore the accusation that we have been undermining this so-called German standard is inconsistent and doesn't stand up," he said.

He urged the parliamentary committee to organise a direct confrontation between Riedinger and all the EU scientists involved in dealing with cattle rendering because he said their integrity had been unfairly attacked.

Hoelgaard also strongly attacked European gelatine manufacturers for withholding important information on the public health risk of methods of making gelatine, which is widely used in jellies, sweets and other confectionery.
The manufacturers only released on June 14 a final report, calling for more research, days after after the Commission had adopted new processing techniques based on an interim report.
"It's a disgrace...undermining their own credibility..," Hoelgaard said, adding that the Commission had had no idea that the findings of the preliminary report would not be confirmed.
